nameStory: The 'Greater Salted Rocktripe' gets its name from its large, leathery appearance that resembles a piece of cow's stomach lining (tripe) growing on rocks. The 'salted' part refers to the white, crusty patches that often appear on its surface, looking like someone sprinkled coarse salt across this rubbery disk.
description: Greater Salted Rocktripe is a large, disk-shaped lichen that grows flat against rock surfaces like a natural leather patch. These remarkable organisms are actually two life forms living together - a fungus and an algae - working as a team to survive on bare rock. Individual specimens can grow 4-8 inches across, forming impressive circular or irregular patches that look almost like giant buttons stuck to cliff faces. They're typically grayish-brown to dark brown in color, with a distinctly leathery, flexible texture when moist.

idTips.label: Single attachment point
idTips.description: Unlike other lichens, this species attaches to rock at just one central point underneath, like a belly button - you can actually lift the edges and feel how it's only connected in the middle

idTips.label: Leathery texture
idTips.description: When wet, feels exactly like soft leather or rubber - pliable and smooth to the touch, not crusty or brittle like many other lichens

idTips.label: White salt-like patches
idTips.description: Look for irregular white or pale gray crusty areas scattered across the surface that feel slightly gritty when rubbed gently with your finger

idTips.label: Large size
idTips.description: One of the biggest lichens you'll encounter - often 4-8 inches across, much larger than most other rock-dwelling lichens

idTips.label: Rock-hugging growth
idTips.description: Grows flush against vertical or slanted rock faces, following every contour and crack like it was poured on as liquid

habitat: Look for Greater Salted Rocktripe on exposed granite and other hard rock outcrops throughout New England's mountains and rocky areas. They thrive on vertical cliff faces and large boulder surfaces that receive good air circulation, often in spots that get morning dew but aren't constantly wet. You'll find them from sea level up to mountain peaks, particularly common on the granite domes and cliffs of New Hampshire's White Mountains and similar rocky terrain throughout the region.

seasonality.spring: Spring rains make specimens plump and leathery - this is the best time to feel their distinctive flexible texture and see their true colors as they become more vibrant when hydrated.
seasonality.summer: During dry summer weather, they shrink and become more brittle and darker, but the white salted patches often become more prominent and easier to spot against the darker background.
seasonality.fall: Cool, moist fall weather revives them after summer dormancy - they'll plump up again and show good color contrast, making identification features more obvious.
seasonality.winter: Remarkably hardy and visible year-round, though they may be brittle when frozen - snow often highlights them by contrast, making them easier to spot on dark rock faces.

funFact: This lichen can completely dry out to a crispy chip for months or even years, appearing totally dead, then come back to life within minutes of getting wet - it's like nature's own freeze-dried food that rehydrates instantly!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Smooth Rock Tripe, but Greater Salted Rocktripe has those distinctive white, salt-like crusty patches scattered across its surface, while Smooth Rock Tripe lives up to its name with a consistently smooth surface. Memory trick: 'Salted' means look for the salt - those white crusty spots are your giveaway.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the unappetizing name 'tripe,' these lichens are actually edible and have been used as emergency food by indigenous peoples and early settlers - though they require extensive preparation and don't taste particularly good. The name can be misleading since this has nothing to do with actual animal tripe beyond the visual similarity.
compareHints: Among New England's rock tripes, Greater Salted Rocktripe stands out for its large size and distinctive white crusty patches. Smooth Rock Tripe lacks these salt-like markings and has a consistently smooth surface, while smaller species like Lesser Rocktripe are typically under 3 inches across. The white patches are really the key feature - no other rock tripe in our region shows this 'salted' appearance as prominently.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's rock tripes, smooth rock tripe lives up to its name with the least textured upper surface.
Lesser Rocktripe is smaller and has a more uniformly wrinkled surface compared to Greater Salted Rocktripe, which can grow much larger and often has distinctive holes or perforations.

Among New England's rock tripes, peppered rock tripe is distinguished by its granular black dots on the surface - smooth rock tripe lacks these entirely, while blistered rock tripe has raised bumps rather than flat granules.

Frosted rock tripe stands out from its rock tripe relatives by its distinctive pale, powdery surface - smooth rock tripe is darker and glossy, while blistered rock tripe has obvious bubble-like bumps.
Blistered Rock Tripe stands out from other rock tripes by its distinctly bumpy, pustule-covered surface - most other species in the genus have smoother tops.
